prompt: What does OSPF use to calculate paths within this single area?
options: A link-state database describing the area topology and costs.
The switch MAC table for every remote LAN.
The router with the highest DR priority as the next hop for every prefix.
Only a list of hop counts reported by the last neighbor.
explanation: Each OSPF router builds the same link-state database and runs SPF from its own position to find the lowest-cost paths.

whyWrong.1: The MAC table is Layer 2 and plays no part in OSPF path calculation.
whyWrong.2: The DR organizes flooding on a segment; it is not the next hop for every route.
whyWrong.3: OSPF uses link costs, not hop counts.

prompt: R3's client LAN is up and passive in OSPF. How does the prefix appear on R3 and on its neighbor R1?
options: Static (S) on R1, because the LAN interface is passive.
Connected (C) on R3 and OSPF-learned (O) on R1.
As a local /32 route only, on both routers.
OSPF-learned (O) on both R3 and R1.
explanation: R3 is attached to the LAN, so it shows a connected (C) route, and R1 learns the prefix from OSPF (O). Passive only stops Hellos on that interface.

whyWrong.0: A passive interface is still advertised, and OSPF routes are never static.
whyWrong.2: OSPF advertises the LAN prefix, not a host route.
whyWrong.3: R3 is directly attached, so its connected route wins over OSPF.

prompt: What does [110/26] mean in this OSPF route?
options: OSPF metric 110 and administrative distance 26.
A /26 prefix learned from router ID 110.
Administrative distance 110 and OSPF metric 26.
A 110-second age and 26-second dead timer.
explanation: The brackets show [administrative distance/metric]. OSPF has distance 110, and 26 is the cost.

whyWrong.0: Distance comes first, then metric.
whyWrong.1: The brackets are not a prefix length or router ID.
whyWrong.3: The brackets are not timers.

prompt: Which TWO values must match for two routers on a broadcast subnet to become OSPFv2 neighbors?
options: Local process ID
Area ID on the link
Router ID
Hello and dead intervals
Interface priority
explanation: Neighbors must agree on the area and on the Hello and dead intervals. Router IDs must differ, and process IDs and priorities can differ.

whyWrong.0: The process ID is local to each router.
whyWrong.2: Router IDs must be unique.
whyWrong.4: Priorities can differ; they only affect DR election.

prompt: R1 Gi0/2 is an up client LAN in area 0 and is passive. Which TWO results are expected?
options: The LAN prefix can be advertised through other OSPF links.
PCs must establish OSPF neighbors before sending traffic.
The interface sends no OSPF Hellos to discover neighbors.
The LAN connected route disappears from R1.
The interface must be shut to keep it passive.
explanation: Passive stops Hellos and neighbor formation on the interface. The LAN prefix is still advertised to other OSPF neighbors.

whyWrong.1: PCs do not run OSPF.
whyWrong.3: The connected route stays while the interface is up.
whyWrong.4: Passive is an OSPF setting and does not shut the interface.

prompt: Which timers are effective on this IOS OSPF interface?
options: Hello 5 seconds and dead 20 seconds.
Hello 10 seconds and dead 40 seconds.
Hello 5 seconds and dead 40 seconds.
Hello 40 seconds and dead 5 seconds.
explanation: Hello is 5 and the dead interval is set explicitly to 40. IOS only derives dead as four times Hello when no dead interval is configured.

whyWrong.0: The explicit dead interval of 40 is used instead of 4 times Hello.
whyWrong.1: The Hello override replaces the default 10 seconds.
whyWrong.3: Hello and dead are reversed.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip ospf hello-interval 5
 ip ospf dead-interval 40

prompt: R1 runs OSPF process 10 and R2 runs process 20. Their link is in area 0 with matching timers and unique RIDs. What happens?
options: They can form an adjacency despite the different process IDs.
They must change both process IDs to area number 0.
They discover each other but stop at 2-Way because of process IDs.
They require identical RIDs to join the same routing process.
explanation: The OSPF process ID is local to each router and does not need to match.

whyWrong.1: Process IDs are unrelated to area numbers.
whyWrong.2: Different process IDs do not stop the adjacency.
whyWrong.3: RIDs must be different, not identical.

prompt: No router-id is configured. Loopback0 is 10.1.1.1 and Loopback1 is 10.9.9.9. Physical interfaces are 172.16.1.1 and 192.168.1.1. Which RID is selected?
options: 10.1.1.1 from the lower-addressed loopback
10.9.9.9 from the higher-addressed loopback
192.168.1.1 from the highest physical address
172.16.1.1 from the first listed physical interface
explanation: With no router-id, IOS uses the highest loopback address. Loopbacks are preferred over physical interfaces.

whyWrong.0: 10.1.1.1 is a loopback but not the highest.
whyWrong.2: Loopbacks are preferred over physical interfaces.
whyWrong.3: Interface order is not the rule.

prompt: Gi0/0 is addressed 172.16.5.33/27. Which router-mode network statement activates only that exact interface address in area 0?
explanation: A wildcard of 0.0.0.0 matches one exact address, which enables OSPF on that interface. OSPF still advertises the interface's real prefix, 172.16.5.32/27.

whyWrong.0: This matches every address in the /27.
whyWrong.1: The command takes a wildcard mask, not a subnet mask.
whyWrong.2: This matches .32, not the interface address .33.

prompt: Which prefix does OSPF advertise for the LAN?
explanation: OSPF advertises the interface's subnet and mask: 192.168.21.33/27 belongs to 192.168.21.32/27.

whyWrong.1: The interface mask is /27, not /24.
whyWrong.2: A host wildcard selects the interface; it does not make the route a /32.
whyWrong.3: The wildcard is not a default route.

exhibit.title: Host wildcard and Ethernet mask (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Gi0/2 up/up: 192.168.21.33/27
router ospf 10
 network 192.168.21.33 0.0.0.0 area 0
 passive-interface Gi0/2

prompt: Which TWO statements about OSPF interface priority 0 are correct?
options: It makes every outgoing route have cost zero.
It forces the current DR to step down in favor of this router.
It makes this interface ineligible for DR and BDR election.
It disables OSPF on the interface.
The router can still become Full with the DR and BDR.
explanation: Priority 0 makes the interface ineligible to be DR or BDR. The router still forms Full adjacencies with the DR and BDR.

whyWrong.0: Priority is not cost.
whyWrong.1: Priority 0 never makes a router the DR.
whyWrong.3: OSPF still runs on the interface.

prompt: R4 is a DROTHER on a healthy four-router broadcast segment. What does its neighbor table show?
options: The 2WAY relationship with R3 is normal for two DROTHERs.
R3 must be changed to point-to-point on this shared segment.
R4 must have a Full adjacency with every router on the segment.
R3 must receive a different process number to complete synchronization.
explanation: DROTHERs stop at 2-Way with each other and form Full adjacencies only with the DR and BDR.

whyWrong.1: The segment should stay broadcast.
whyWrong.2: Two DROTHERs do not become Full with each other.
whyWrong.3: Process IDs are local and do not cause this state.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R4# show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri State          Address       Interface
1.1.1.1         100 FULL/DR        10.0.123.1    Gi0/0
2.2.2.2          50 FULL/BDR       10.0.123.2    Gi0/0
3.3.3.3           1 2WAY/DROTHER   10.0.123.3    Gi0/0

prompt: No DR or BDR exists and all four routers start an election. Who becomes DR and BDR?
options: RB is DR; RD is BDR.
RA is DR; RC is BDR.
RD is DR; RC is BDR.
RD is DR; RA is BDR.
explanation: Highest priority wins DR, so RD with 50. RA and RC tie on priority 1, and RA wins BDR with the higher RID.

whyWrong.0: RB has priority 0, so it is ineligible.
whyWrong.1: RD has a higher priority than RA and RC.
whyWrong.2: RA and RC tie on priority, and RA has the higher RID.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
Candidate  Interface priority  RID
RA         1                   4.4.4.4
RB         0                   9.9.9.9
RC         1                   3.3.3.3
RD         50                  1.1.1.1

prompt: R1 is the DR and R2 is the BDR. R3 joins later with priority 200, then R1 fails. What happens?
options: R3 becomes DR immediately when it joins.
R2 becomes DR, and R3 can become BDR.
R2 remains BDR while R3 and the remaining DROTHERs run a fresh DR-only comparison.
R3 becomes DR after R1 fails, bypassing R2.
explanation: DR election does not preempt. When the DR fails, the BDR becomes DR, and a new BDR is elected.

whyWrong.0: A later joiner does not take over an existing DR.
whyWrong.2: The BDR is promoted when the DR fails.
whyWrong.3: The BDR is promoted before any new election.

prompt: R1 reaches a LAN through R2 then R3. Outgoing costs are R1 to R2 = 10, R2 to R3 = 20 and R3 to the LAN = 1. What metric does R1 calculate?
explanation: OSPF adds the outgoing interface costs along the path: 10 + 20 + 1 = 31.

whyWrong.1: This leaves out the last link to the LAN.
whyWrong.2: This leaves out R1's outgoing cost.
whyWrong.3: 110 is the administrative distance.

prompt: Which command on every OSPF router gives 100-Mbps, 1-Gbps and 10-Gbps interfaces costs of 100, 10 and 1?
options: auto-cost reference-bandwidth 1000
auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000
ip ospf priority 100
auto-cost reference-bandwidth 100
explanation: Cost is reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth. A reference of 10000 Mbps gives 100, 10 and 1.

whyWrong.0: A 1000 reference gives costs 10, 1 and 1.
whyWrong.2: Priority affects DR election, not cost.
whyWrong.3: The 100 default gives costs 1, 1 and 1.

prompt: What cost does OSPF use for this outgoing interface?
explanation: An explicit ip ospf cost overrides the automatic calculation.

whyWrong.0: 1000 is the reference bandwidth, not the cost.
whyWrong.1: 100 is the interface bandwidth, not the cost.
whyWrong.2: 10 is the automatic cost, but the explicit cost overrides it.

exhibit.title: Automatic and explicit cost settings (exercise)
exhibit.text:
OSPF reference bandwidth: 1000 Mbps
Interface configured bandwidth: 100 Mbps
Interface command: ip ospf cost 7

prompt: R1 sends a packet to R3's client LAN across a shared Ethernet where R2 is the DR. What is the next hop?
options: R3's shared-interface address, even though R2 is the DR.
The destination PC's MAC address, learned across the routed LAN.
The DR's address for every packet, whichever router owns the destination.
The BDR's address, because only the backup forwards user traffic.
explanation: The DR and BDR handle LSA exchange, not user traffic. R1 sends directly to R3's address on the segment.

whyWrong.1: The next hop is the router on the shared segment, not a remote PC.
whyWrong.2: The DR does not forward other routers' traffic.
whyWrong.3: The BDR is a control role and does not forward traffic.

exhibit.title: Shared Ethernet forwarding path (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1, R2 and R3 share 10.0.123.0/24. R2 is DR.
R3 advertises its client LAN.
The shortest path from R1 to that LAN crosses the shared segment directly to R3; there are no filters.

prompt: You configure a new router-id on a router that has OSPF neighbors, but show ip ospf still shows the old RID. What should you do?
options: Assign the same new RID to every router to keep the area consistent.
Plan a maintenance window and run clear ip ospf process, then confirm the RID.
Assume the new running-config value already changed every adjacency identity.
Change all neighbor process IDs to the new RID.
explanation: IOS keeps the RID chosen at process start. Run clear ip ospf process in a maintenance window, because it drops adjacencies.

whyWrong.0: Router IDs must be unique.
whyWrong.2: The running RID does not change until the process restarts.
whyWrong.3: Process IDs are not router IDs.

prompt: R2's transit interface is up/up and addressed, but there is no neighbor on it. Which line explains this?
options: passive-interface default without a Gi0/0 exception
router-id 2.2.2.2 in the routing process
router ospf 20 rather than process 10
explanation: passive-interface default stops Hellos on every interface unless you add no passive-interface for the transit link.

whyWrong.1: An explicit unique RID is normal.
whyWrong.2: This statement correctly enables the interface.
whyWrong.3: Neighbors can use different process IDs.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
router ospf 20
 router-id 2.2.2.2
 passive-interface default
 network 10.0.123.2 0.0.0.0 area 0

prompt: A cloned router configuration produces the log below. What fixes it?
options: Give every router a different local process number.
Raise the new router interface election priority.
Put each shared-interface peer in a different area.
Assign unique explicit RIDs and apply any required controlled process restart.
explanation: The log shows a duplicate router ID. Give each router a unique router-id and restart the process to apply it.

whyWrong.0: Process IDs are not router IDs.
whyWrong.1: Priority affects DR election only.
whyWrong.2: Putting neighbors in different areas stops the adjacency.

prompt: The client LAN is missing from OSPF while the transit adjacency works. What is the repair?
options: Remove passive status from Gi0/2 but leave it outside OSPF.
Activate Gi0/2 in area 0 and keep it passive toward clients.
Raise the transit DR priority to advertise more LANs.
Change the transit process number to match the neighbor.
explanation: The LAN interface was never enabled in OSPF. Activate it in area 0 and keep it passive toward clients.

whyWrong.0: Passive is not an activation setting.
whyWrong.2: DR priority does not enable an interface in OSPF.
whyWrong.3: Process IDs do not need to match.

exhibit.title: Connected LAN outside OSPF (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Gi0/2 up/up: 192.168.25.1/24; local PC can reach it.
Only Gi0/0 has ip ospf 10 area 0.
OSPF process 10: passive-interface default; no passive-interface Gi0/0
Gi0/0 neighbor is Full; no network statements or redistribution.
The neighbor has no route to 192.168.25.0/24.

prompt: Which change fixes the OSPF activation mismatch?
options: Widen the actual LAN mask to /24 so the mistaken selector appears to cover it.
Change the LAN selection so that it includes 192.168.31.65, retaining area 0 and the intended /27.
Set the PC default gateway to the neighboring router transit IP.
Lower the reference bandwidth to advertise the missing prefix.
explanation: The wildcard 0.0.0.31 at .32 covers .32 to .63, but the interface is .65 in 192.168.31.64/27. Change the network statement to include it.

whyWrong.0: Changing the mask abandons the subnet plan.
whyWrong.2: The gateway is not the problem.
whyWrong.3: Cost does not control whether an interface runs OSPF.

exhibit.title: LAN prefix and wildcard selection (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Required LAN: 192.168.31.64/27
R1 Gi0/2: 192.168.31.65/27 up/up
Only LAN selector: network 192.168.31.32 0.0.0.31 area 0
Gi0/2 is passive; transit adjacency is Full; remote router lacks this LAN.
No interface-level OSPF activation is present.

prompt: R1 stays in Init with R2. What should you check next?
options: Increase R1 DR priority so its Hello will include itself as a neighbor.
Check whether R2 receives R1 Hellos and lists R1 RID in its own Hellos.
Assume all Init states are caused by mismatched MTU.
Change both router IDs to the same value so the Hello names match.
explanation: Init means R1 hears R2, but R2's Hellos do not list R1. Check whether R2 receives R1's Hellos and accepts them.

whyWrong.0: Priority does not fix one-way Hello recognition.
whyWrong.2: MTU problems show up later, at ExStart.
whyWrong.3: Router IDs must be unique.

exhibit.title: Persistent one-way Hello recognition (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1 repeatedly sees R2 in INIT.
R1 receives R2 Hellos, but those Hellos do not list R1 RID.
Interfaces are up. No capture or filter inspection at R2 has yet been collected.

prompt: Which routes result from the directed costs?
options: R1 uses the shared path at cost 21; R3 uses the direct path at cost 31.
R1 uses the direct path at cost 6; R3 uses the shared path at cost 11.
Both use the direct path at cost 6 because the physical link is shared.
Both use the shared path because a DR is present there.
explanation: Each router adds its own outgoing costs and picks the lower total. R1 compares 6 with 21, and R3 compares 31 with 11.

whyWrong.0: Both routers would be choosing the higher total.
whyWrong.2: Costs are set per direction, so each router picks its own lowest.
whyWrong.3: The DR does not change path costs.

exhibit.title: Directed OSPF costs (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Area 0, all adjacencies Full, no other paths.
R1 -> shared Ethernet: 20; R3 -> shared Ethernet: 10
R1 -> R3 direct point-to-point: 5; R3 -> R1 direct: 30
LAN-A on R1 cost 1; LAN-B on R3 cost 1
Compare R1 route to LAN-B and R3 route to LAN-A.

prompt: Both paths are eligible and maximum-paths allows two. What happens?
options: The two costs add together and create one cost-32 route.
The lower-bandwidth path must be rejected even when the explicit costs tie.
Both next hops can install at cost 16; equal throughput is not guaranteed.
Only the next hop with the higher router ID is installed.
explanation: Equal-cost paths are installed together without adding their costs. Both next hops install at cost 16.

whyWrong.0: Parallel path costs are not added.
whyWrong.1: The explicit costs decide, so a tie is a tie.
whyWrong.3: Equal-cost routes are installed together, not by RID.

exhibit.title: Two eligible paths to one prefix (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Path A: R1 outgoing 5 + R2 outgoing 10 + remote LAN 1
Path B: R1 outgoing 15 + remote LAN 1
Both advertise the same intra-area prefix; no other route source wins.

prompt: A static route to a prefix is installed. Does that show OSPF did not learn the prefix?
options: Yes; a prefix cannot exist in both OSPF information and the routing table from another source.
Yes; OSPF administrative distance 110 always beats static distance 1.
No; OSPF must instead install the same prefix as a connected route.
No; the lower-distance static can win installation even when OSPF knows the same prefix.
explanation: Static distance 1 beats OSPF distance 110, so the static route installs even if OSPF knows the prefix. Check the OSPF database separately.

whyWrong.0: OSPF can know a prefix that another source wins.
whyWrong.1: Lower distance wins, and static is 1.
whyWrong.2: Connected routes are not copies of learned routes.

exhibit.title: Installed route source (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Installed: S 192.168.26.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2
OSPF adjacency to R2 is Full.
An engineer claims that the S code alone proves R2 never advertised this LAN.

prompt: R1 and R3 are the only routers on an Ethernet link and report Full, but remote LAN routes are missing. What should you fix first?
options: Change R3 process 30 to process 10.
Configure the same intended OSPF network type at both ends.
Change both interfaces to Hello 30 and dead 120.
Replace the /30 addressing with a /24 subnet.
explanation: Both ends must use the same OSPF network type. The exhibit shows broadcast on one end and point-to-point on the other.

whyWrong.0: Process IDs can differ.
whyWrong.2: The timers already agree.
whyWrong.3: The /30 addressing is valid.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1: 10.0.13.1/30, Area 0, Process 10, Network Type BROADCAST
    Hello 10, Dead 40
R3: 10.0.13.2/30, Area 0, Process 30, Network Type POINT_TO_POINT
    Hello 10, Dead 40

prompt: The adjacency never reaches Full. What does the evidence show?
options: Point-to-point operation omits the required DR.
The two process numbers are different.
The interface MTU values differ.
The peer uses a unique router ID.
explanation: DBD packets carry the interface MTU, and a mismatch keeps the neighbors in ExStart or Exchange. Make the MTUs equal.

whyWrong.0: Point-to-point links do not need a DR.
whyWrong.1: Process IDs can differ.
whyWrong.3: Unique RIDs are required.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R1 Gi0/1: up/up, MTU 1500, area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40
R2 Gi0/1: up/up, MTU 1400, area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40
R1 shows neighbor 2.2.2.2 in EXCHANGE/ -
R2 shows neighbor 1.1.1.1 in EXSTART/ -

prompt: What does the successful ping not show?
options: It cannot establish any end-to-end reachability at all.
It does not establish that the direct backup adjacency is healthy.
It proves the direct link is carrying the ping because the routers are neighbors elsewhere.
It proves the two timer settings are compatible.
explanation: A ping that succeeds over another path says nothing about the direct link's adjacency. Check each interface's neighbor and route.

whyWrong.0: The ping does show end-to-end reachability for that pair.
whyWrong.2: The route uses the shared interface, not the direct link.
whyWrong.3: The ping does not test timer compatibility.

exhibit.title: Working primary and failed backup adjacency (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1 shared Gi0/0 route to LAN-B: cost 11, neighbor Full.
R1 direct Gi0/1: Hello/dead 5/20; no neighbor.
R3 direct Gi0/1: Hello/dead 10/40.
PC-A successfully pings PC-B through the shared path.

prompt: Which IP protocol number does OSPF use?
explanation: OSPF runs directly over IP as protocol 89, with no TCP or UDP port.

whyWrong.0: 6 is TCP.
whyWrong.1: 17 is UDP.
whyWrong.3: 88 is EIGRP.

prompt: Which multicast address reaches all OSPFv2 routers?
explanation: 224.0.0.5 is the all-OSPF-routers address, used for Hellos.

whyWrong.1: 224.0.0.6 reaches only the DR and BDR.

prompt: What are the default Hello and dead intervals on an OSPF broadcast interface?
options: 5 and 20 seconds
10 and 40 seconds
30 and 120 seconds
40 and 10 seconds
explanation: The defaults are Hello 10 seconds and dead 40 seconds.

whyWrong.0: 5 and 20 are not the defaults.
whyWrong.2: 30 and 120 are the defaults on non-broadcast networks.
whyWrong.3: Hello is shorter than dead, not longer.

prompt: What is the default OSPF interface priority?
explanation: The default OSPF interface priority is 1. Priority 0 makes the router ineligible for DR and BDR.

whyWrong.0: 0 means the router cannot be DR or BDR.
whyWrong.2: 100 is not a default.
whyWrong.3: 255 is the highest value, not the default.
